verses.zh: 哀哉！我（或译：以色列）好像夏天的果子已被收尽，又像摘了葡萄所剩下的，没有一挂可吃的；我心羡慕初熟的无花果。
verses.en: Woe is me!For I am like those gathering fruitand those harvesting grapes,when there is no grape cluster to eatand no fresh figs that my stomach[NOTE:1] craves.
notes: Heb “appetite, soul.”

verses.zh: 地上虔诚人灭尽；世间没有正直人；各人埋伏，要杀人流血，都用网罗猎取弟兄。
verses.en: Faithful men have disappeared[NOTE:1] from the land;there are no godly men left.[NOTE:2] They all wait in ambush to shed blood;[NOTE:3] they hunt their own brother with a net.
notes: Or “have perished.”
Heb “and an upright one among men there is not.”
Heb “for bloodshed” (so NASB); TEV “for a chance to commit murder.”

verses.zh: 他们双手作恶；君王徇情面，审判官要贿赂；位分大的吐出恶意，都彼此结联行恶。
verses.en: They are experts at doing evil;[NOTE:1] government officials and judges take bribes,[NOTE:2] prominent men announce what they wish, and then they plan it out.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “their hands [reach] to evil to do [it] well,” or with slight emendation “their hands are skillful at doing evil.”
Heb “the official asks—and the judge—for a bribe.”

More literally, “the great one announces what his appetite desires and they weave it together.” Apparently this means that subordinates plot and maneuver to make sure the prominent man’s desires materialize.

verses.zh: 他们最好的，不过是蒺藜；最正直的，不过是荆棘篱笆。你守望者说，降罚的日子已经来到。他们必扰乱不安。
verses.en: The best of them is like a thorn;their godly are like a thornbush.[NOTE:1] Woe[NOTE:2] to your watchmen; your appointed punishment is on the way.[NOTE:3] The time of their confusion is now.[NOTE:4]
notes: The MT reads יָשָׁר מִמְּסוּכָה (yashar mimmesukhah) “a godly [person] from a thorn bush.” Theoretically the preposition מִן (min, “from”) could be comparative (“more than”), but it would need an attributive adjective for this meaning. Most likely this is a case of wrong word division, where the מ (mem) is not מִן (min, “from”), but is actually a third masculine plural pronominal suffix, similar to the first clause (“their best”). The line would read יְשָׁרָם מְסוּכָה (yesharam mesukhah) “their upright person is a thorn bush.”

The text is uncertain at several points. Where the MT reads יוֹם (yom, “day [of]”), the LXX reads οὐαὶ (ouai, “woe”) implying הוֹי (hoi, “woe”). The watchmen may be actual sentries or symbolic of true of false prophets. If reading with the MT, the “day of your watchmen,” might be the day they are on the lookout for, or the day they have announced. Reading “woe” either warns the sentries on the lookout or rebukes false prophets.
Or “has come.”
Heb “Now will be their confusion.”

verses.zh: 不要倚赖邻舍；不要信靠密友。要守住你的口；不要向你怀中的妻提说。
verses.en: Do not rely on a friend;do not trust a companion!Even with the one who lies in your arms,do not share secrets![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “guard the doors of your mouth.”

verses.zh: 因为，儿子藐视父亲；女儿抗拒母亲；媳妇抗拒婆婆；人的仇敌就是自己家里的人。
verses.en: For a son thinks his father is a fool,a daughter challenges[NOTE:1] her mother,and a daughter-in-law her mother-in-law;a man’s enemies are his own family.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “rises up against.”
Heb “his house.” Household may include servants as well as family.

verses.zh: 至于我，我要仰望耶和华，要等候那救我的　神；我的　神必应允我。
verses.en: But I will keep watching for the Lord;I will wait for the God who delivers me.My God will listen to me.

verses.zh: 我的仇敌啊，不要向我夸耀。我虽跌倒，却要起来；我虽坐在黑暗里，耶和华却作我的光。
verses.en: My enemies,[NOTE:1] do not gloat[NOTE:2] over me!Though I have fallen, I will get up.Though I sit in darkness, the Lord will be my light.[NOTE:3]
notes: The singular form is understood as collective.
Or “rejoice” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); NCV “don’t laugh at me.”
Darkness represents judgment; light (also in v. 9) symbolizes deliverance.

verses.zh: 我要忍受耶和华的恼怒；因我得罪了他，直等他为我辨屈，为我伸冤。他必领我到光明中；我必得见他的公义。
verses.en: I must endure[NOTE:1] the Lord’s fury,for I have sinned against him.But then[NOTE:2] he will defend my cause[NOTE:3] and accomplish justice on my behalf.He will lead me out into the light;I will witness his deliverance.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “bear, carry.”
Heb “until.”
Or “plead my case” (NASB and NIV both similar); NRSV “until he takes my side.”
Or “justice, vindication.”

verses.zh: 那时我的仇敌，就是曾对我说「耶和华―你　神在哪里」的，他一看见这事就被羞愧遮盖。我必亲眼见他遭报；他必被践踏，如同街上的泥土。
verses.en: When my enemies see this, they will be covered with shame.They say[NOTE:1] to me, “Where is the Lord your God?”I will gloat over them;[NOTE:2] then they will be trampled down[NOTE:3] like mud in the streets.
notes: Heb “who say.” A new sentence was begun here in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “My eyes will look on them.”
Heb “a trampled-down place.”

verses.zh: 以色列啊，日子必到，你的墙垣必重修；到那日，你的境界必开展（或译：命令必传到远方）。
verses.en: It will be a day for rebuilding your walls;in that day your boundary will be extended.[NOTE:1]
notes: Personified Jerusalem declares her confidence in vv. 8-10; in this verse she is assured that she will indeed be vindicated.

verses.zh: 当那日，人必从亚述，从埃及的城邑，从埃及到大河，从这海到那海，从这山到那山，都归到你这里。
verses.en: In that day people[NOTE:1] will come to you[NOTE:2] from Assyria as far as[NOTE:3] Egypt,from Egypt as far as the Euphrates River,[NOTE:4] from the seacoasts[NOTE:5] and the mountains.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “he.” The referent has been specified as “people,” referring either to the nations (coming to God with their tribute) or to the exiles of Israel (returning to the Lord).
The masculine pronominal suffix suggests the Lord is addressed. Some emend to a feminine form and take Jerusalem as the addressee.
The MT reads וְעָרֵי (veʿarey, “and the cities [of Egypt]”), but the parallel line indicates this needs emendation to וְעַד (veʿad, “even to”).
Heb “the River,” referring to the Euphrates River (so also NASB, NIV).
Heb “and sea from sea.” Many prefer to emend this to מִיָּם עַד יָם (miyyam ʿad yam, “from sea to sea”).
Heb “and mountain of the mountain.” Many prefer to emend this to וּמֵהַר עַד הַר (umehar ʿad har, “and mountain to mountain”).

verses.zh: 然而，这地因居民的缘故，又因他们行事的结果，必然荒凉。
verses.en: The earth will become desolatebecause of what its inhabitants have done.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “on account of its inhabitants, because of the fruit of their deeds.”

verses.zh: 求耶和华在迦密山的树林中，用你的杖牧放你独居的民，就是你产业的羊群。求你容他们在巴珊和基列得食物，像古时一样。
verses.en: Shepherd your people with your rod,[NOTE:1] the flock that belongs to you,[NOTE:2] the one that lives alone in a thicket,in the midst of a pastureland.[NOTE:3] Allow them to graze in Bashan and Gilead,[NOTE:4] as they did in the old days.[NOTE:5]
notes: The Hebrew term שֵׁבֶט (shevet) can refer to a rod, such as a ṣhepherd’s rod, or a “scepter.”
Heb “the flock of your inheritance.”

Or “in the midst of Carmel.” The Hebrew term translated “pastureland” may be a place name.sn The point seems to be that Israel is in a vulnerable position, like sheep in a thicket populated by predators, while rich pastureland (their homeland and God’s blessings) is in view.
The regions of Bashan and Gilead, located in Transjordan, were noted for their rich grazing lands.
Heb “as in the days of antiquity.”

verses.zh: 耶和华说：我要把奇事显给他们看，好像出埃及地的时候一样。
verses.en: “As in the days when you departed from the land of Egypt,I will show you[NOTE:1] miraculous deeds.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “him.” This probably refers to Israel in a collective sense. Because the switch from direct address to the third person is awkward, some prefer to emend the suffix to a second person form. In any case, it is necessary to employ a second person pronoun in the translation to maintain the connection for the English reader.
I will show you miraculous deeds. In this verse the Lord responds to the petition of v. 14 with a brief promise of deliverance.

verses.zh: 列国看见这事就必为自己的势力惭愧；他们必用手捂口，掩耳不听。
verses.en: Nations will see this and be disappointed by[NOTE:1] all their strength;they will put their hands over their mouthsand act as if they were deaf.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “be ashamed of.”
Heb “and their ears will be deaf.” Apparently this means the opposing nations will be left dumbfounded by the Lord’s power. Their inability to respond will make them appear to be deaf mutes.

verses.zh: 他们必舔土如蛇，又如土中腹行的物，战战兢兢地出他们的营寨。他们必战惧投降耶和华，也必因我们的　神而惧怕。
verses.en: They will lick the dust like a snake,like serpents crawling on the ground.[NOTE:1] They will come trembling from their strongholdsto the Lord our God;[NOTE:2] they will be terrified[NOTE:3] of you.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “like crawling things on the ground.” The parallelism suggests snakes are in view.

The translation assumes that the phrase אֶל־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ (ʾel yehvah ʾelohenu, “to the Lord our God”) goes with what precedes. Another option is to take the phrase with the following verb, in which case one could translate, “to the Lord our God they will turn in dread.”
Heb “they will be in dread and afraid.”
The Lord is addressed directly using the second person.

verses.zh: 神啊，有何神像你，赦免罪孽，饶恕你产业之余民的罪过，不永远怀怒，喜爱施恩？
verses.en: Who is a God like you?[NOTE:1] Who[NOTE:2] forgives sinand pardons[NOTE:3] the rebellionof those who remain among his people?[NOTE:4] Who does not stay angry forever,but delights in showing loyal love?
notes: The rhetorical question expects the answer, “No one!” The claim is supported by the following description.

Heb “one who,” a substantival participle. The descriptions in the rest of vv. 18-19 fill out the rhetorical question, “Who is a God like you?” That is, they provide descriptions of God as reasons that make him without equal. This context uses two participles, e.g. “who forgives” and “who pardons,” and then independent clauses with third person verbs. A similar construction occurs in Ps 113:5-9, with participles and a third person finite verb in v. 7. Here, making the two participles grammatically dependent on the rhetorical question and then switching to the third person is confusing English style. It masks that all these descriptions are serving the same function as a list of unique qualities of God, who is addressed in the second person. To tie these together in English, all the descriptions can be made into second person statements (so NIV), though this does not clarify the distinction of when the original text deliberately switches back to second person in v. 20. Another approach would be to translate the third person clauses as indefinite and dependent, e.g. “Who is…like you, someone who does X, someone who does Y?” Or the interrogative force can be be extended, e.g. “Who is the one who does not stay angry?”
Heb “passes over.”
Heb “of the remnant of his inheritance.”

verses.zh: 必再怜悯我们，将我们的罪孽踏在脚下，又将我们的一切罪投于深海。
verses.en: Who[NOTE:1] will once again[NOTE:2] have mercy on us?Who will conquer[NOTE:3] our evil deeds?Who will hurl[NOTE:4] all our[NOTE:5] sins into the depths of the sea?[NOTE:6]
notes: The interrogative force of the previous verse is continued here, part of a list of attributes reinforcing the question, “Who is like God?”
The verb יָשׁוּב (yashuv, “he will return”) is here used adverbially in relation to the following verb, indicating that the Lord will again show mercy.
Some prefer to read יִכְבֹּס (yikhbos, “he will cleanse”; see HALOT 459 s.v. כבס pi). If the MT is taken as it stands, sin is personified as an enemy that the Lord subdues.

The MT reads וְתַשְׁלִיך (vetashlik, “and you will throw”), while the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate read “he will throw,” implying וְהַשְׁלִיך (vehashlik). Being conceptually tied to the previous verb, this one should be part of the list begun in v. 18, so the third person form is expected. Also the vav plus perfect consecutive is more typical than vav plus imperfect in this setting.

Heb “their sins.” The LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate read “our sins.” The shape of the letters in the first person plural suffix נו (nun and vav) look very much like ם (a final mem), which makes the third person plural suffix. Confusing the two is not an uncommon copying error. It may also be an enclitic ם rather than a pronominal suffix. In that case the suffix from the preceding line (“our”) may be understood as doing double duty.
In this metaphor the Lord disposes of Israel’s sins by throwing them into the waters of the sea (here symbolic of chaos).

verses.zh: 你必按古时起誓应许我们列祖的话，向雅各发诚实，向亚伯拉罕施慈爱。
verses.en: You will be loyal to Jacoband extend your loyal love to Abraham,[NOTE:1] which you promised on oath to our ancestors[NOTE:2] in ancient times.[NOTE:3]
notes: More literally, “You will extend loyalty to Jacob, and loyal love to Abraham.”
Heb “our fathers,” meaning “our forefathers.”
Heb “from days of old.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This chapter can be analyzed by who is speaking and who is being spoken to. See note at Micah 7:1.

- The NIV Bible outlines the speakers as

- Micah, Micah 7:1-7, 11-13, 16-20

- Zion, Micah 7:8-10, 14

- YHWH, Micah 7:15

- It is difficult

- to separate the prophet speaking and YHWH speaking

- because Hebrew poetry changes SUBJECTS and PRONOUNS
(i.e. SINGULAR, PLURAL) often for literary effect

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: MICAH 7:1-6

1"Woe is me! For I am

Like the fruit pickers and the grape gatherers.

There is not a cluster of grapes to eat,

Or a first-ripe fig which I crave.

2The godly person has perished from the land,

And there is no upright person among men.

All of them lie in wait for bloodshed;

Each of them hunts the other with a net.

3Concerning evil, both hands do it well.

The prince asks, also the judge, for a bribe,

And a great man speaks the desire of his soul;

So they weave it together.

4The best of them is like a briar,

The most upright like a thorn hedge.

The day when you post a watchman,

Your punishment will come.

Then their confusion will occur.

5Do not trust in a neighbor;

Do not have confidence in a friend.

From her who lies in your bosom

Guard your lips.

6For son treats father contemptuously,

Daughter rises up against her mother,

Daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law;

A man's enemies are the men of his own household.

7:1 "Woe is me!" This is an individual lament (BDB 47), although at times it moves into the area of a
corporate plea. This is a common literary technique of the Psalms (cf. Ps. 5; 13; 22; 55; 71).

It is uncertain who is speaking:

- the prophet himself

- the prophet as YHWH's spokesperson

- the prophet on behalf of the godly remnant

- Samaria (JPSOA footnote, "the speaker is FEMININE, cf. Micah 6:16). Remember, Isaiah and
Micah are 8th century prophets. Assyria was the immediate threat.

▣

NASB
"I am like the fruit pickers"

NKJV, REB, Peshitta
"For I am like those who gather

summer fruit"

NRSV
"For I have become like one who, after

the summer fruit has been gathered"

TEV
"I am like a hungry person who finds

no fruit"

NJB
"a harvester in summer time"

JPSOA
"I am become like leavings of a fig

harvest"

LXX
"I have become like one gathering

stubble at the harvest"

The NASB has left out the term "summer" (BDB 884) which denotes "heat." This gathering is not
the initial harvest, but the last pickings of the post-harvest season. YHWH waited and waited for fruit, but there
was never a harvest (cf. Isaiah 5)!

▣ "Like the fruit-pickers and the grape gatherers" Micah craves righteousness (or a righteous people
or righteous leadership, i.e. Micah 7:3) as a hungry man craves food (cf. Matt. 5:6). The concept of righteousness as food
is found throughout the Bible (cf. Amos 6:12; John 15:1-8; Phil. 1:11; Gal. 5:23).

The Jewish Publication Society of America (JPSOA) says Micah 7:1 refers to Samaria. They search for
food, but cannot find it because of

- the siege

- YHWH's famine, cf. Deuteronomy 27-28)

The JPSOA continues this thought through Micah 7:7.

However, I think this context relates to Jerusalem.

- in one sense they are too late (i.e. the harvest of their unrighteousness has occurred—exile)

- in another sense they are too early (i.e. the promise of restoration in the future has not yet come)

▣ "first ripe fig, which I crave" These early figs were very sweet and sought after. They first appeared
in June, although, the major harvest did not occur until August. Micah (as YHWH's spokesman) is searching for righteousness
as a man longs for these first figs.

7:2 "The godly person" This is the ADJECTIVE (BDB339) form of the covenant term, hesed, which
means YHWH's unconditional, no strings attached, covenant loyalty (e.g. Micah 7:18; 6:8; 7:18; Jer. 5:1). It is parallel to "upright
person." This is referring to a covenantly faithful person, of which there is none (e.g. Ps. 12:1; Isa. 57:1)!

Special Topic: Lovingkindness (hesed)

▣ "All of them lie in wait for bloodshed" The VERB (BDB 70, KB 83) is a Qal
IMPERFECT, which denotes continual action and is used often in Joshua and Judges and is translated "ambush." This is imagery of
hunting to describe the scheming violence of the elite of the covenant people (i.e. the greedy, wealthy, powerful leaders).

▣

NASB
"bloodshed"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta, LXX
"blood"

TEV, REB
"murder"

JPSOA
"commit crimes"

This term (BDB 196) is literally "blood." It is used often by the eighth century prophets (mostly
Ezekiel, cf. Hosea 1:4; 4:2; 6:8; 12:14; Jonah 1:14; Micah 3:10) to describe violence and death.

Special Topic: Blood

▣ "Each of them hunts the other with a net" They exploit each other at every opportunity. Their motto
would be "more and more for me at any cost!" Persons made in God's image, covenant partners, have no value in their eyes!

7:3 "Concerning evil, both hands do it well" This is another striking allusion to ambidextrous evil. The
VERB (BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) means to do something
well or thoroughly. Here a word normally used of doing something good is used of planned, purposeful evil!

▣ "The prince asks, also the judge, for a bribe" The leaders were seeking personal gain (i.e. bribe, cf. Micah 3:11;
Exod. 23:8; Deut. 10:17; 16:19; 27:25; Isa. 1:23) instead of justice.

▣ "And a great man speaks the desire of his soul;

So they weave it together" This verse describes the corrupt judicial and political
situation (cf. Micah 3:1-12; Isa. 59:9-12; Jer. 8:8-12; 22; 23; 26:12-15). The wealthy man tells the judges and governmental
officials what he wants and they find a way to get it for him, no matter what it takes. God's covenant people have
become corrupt. They look and act just like all other fallen nations!

The VERB "weave" (BDB 721, KB 783, Piel IMPERFECT)
is found only here. The related form is found in Joel 2:7 as "deviate" or "swerve." This term may be a play on the
concept of sin as a deviation from God's standard (i.e. righteousness).

Special Topic: Righteousness

7:4 This seems to be sarcasm (cf. JPSOA translation), but it is possibly related to the idea that everything
they tried to do to prepare for invasion did not work (cf. Isa. 22:5). There seems to be a change of subject in Micah 7:4.

The first two lines describe the ungodly mentioned in Micah 7:2-3. However, the next three lines may refer to

- the prophets (watchmen, cf. Jer. 6:17; Ezek. 3:17; Hosea 9:8)

- Judah's preparations for siege

For a good brief discussion of "thorns" see UBS Fauna anda Flora of the Bible, pp. 184-186.

▣ "confusion" This term (BDB 100) is used to describe YHWH's judgment (e.g. Isa. 22:5).

7:5-6 These verses show

- the level of corruption that had occurred within Judean society (i.e. cannot trust neighbors, friends, family)

- the stress caused by the siege

Everyone was out for personal gain (cf. Micah 7:2-3; Jer. 9:4; 12:6). There were no true friends (i.e. Prov. 17:17; 27:6,9).

This verse has two IMPERFECTS used as JUSSIVES and one
IMPERATIVE:

- "do not trust" ‒ BDB 52, KB 63, Hiphil IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE

- "do not have confidence" ‒ BDB 105, KB 120, Qal IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE

- "guard" ‒ BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERATIVE

Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the OT, p. 102, has a good discussion of the uses of the Hebrew root אמן.

- in ACTIVE stem ‒ to nurse or nourish

- in PASSIVE stem ‒ to be firm, steadfast

- in CAUSATIVE stem ‒ to take as established, or true

Special Topic: Believe, Trust, Faith and Faithfulness

7:6 "son treats father contemptuously" The VERB (BDB 614, KB 663, Piel PARTICIPLE)
means "treat with contempt," "dishonor," or "scoff" (e.g. Deut. 32:15; Jer. 14:21; Nahum 3:6). This is a violation of the Ten Words
(cf. Exod. 20:12). This imagery is also used in
the NT in an eschatological sense (cf. Matt. 10:35-36; Mark 13:12; Luke 12:53). God knows how this feels (cf. Micah 2:18).

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: MICAH 7:7-8

7"But as for me, I will watch expectantly for the Lord;

I will wait for the God of my salvation.

My God will hear me.

8Do not rejoice over me, O my enemy.

Though I fall I will rise;

Though I dwell in darkness, the Lord is a light for me.

7:7 "I will watch expectantly for the Lord" Notice the sharp contrast between Micah 7:7
and Micah 7:1-6. The VERB (BDB 859, KB 1044, Piel IMPERFECT) is used in a
COHORTATIVE sense. Patient trusting in YHWH's actions is evidence of faith (e.g. Ps. 38:15; 39:7; 42:5;
130:5; Isa. 8:17; Lam. 3:25).

▣ "I will wait for the God of my salvation" What a wonderful title for YHWH (e.g. Ps. 25:5; 79:9; Isa. 12:2;
Hab. 3:18). Notice the personal element ("my") in the divine title. The VERB (BDB 403, KB 407) is a
Hiphil COHORTATIVE; the remnant waits patiently and YHWH acts decisively. These two (three)
poetic lines are parallel and describe a faithful, trusting, covenant follower of YHWH.

Special Topic: Descriptive Titles for God

Special Topic: Salvation (OT Term)

Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses), A. #3

▣ "My God will hear me" Micah has previously announced that YHWH will not hear and respond to the
prayers of evil Israelites or Judeans (e.g. Micah 3:4), but He will surely hear and respond to those who keep His covenant in faith (cf. Micah 6:8).

7:8-13 The interpretive question is, "Does Micah 7:8 go with Micah 7:7 or start a new strophe?" Most English
translations start a new thought at Micah 7:8 (NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, but not NASB).

It seems that Micah 7:8-10 may need to be separate from Micah 7:11-13 because the last two verses
reflect the will of YHWH for future restoration and universal influence. The NET Bible, p. 1630, #15,
suggests vv. 8-10 reflect personified Jerusalem.

7:8 "Do not rejoice over me" The VERB (BDB 403, KB 407) is a Hiphpael
COHORTATIVE. The immediate judgment of YHWH will one day be reversed!

▣ "O my enemy" The enemy here could be the invading nations (JPSOA footnote, Heb. FEMININE,
apparently referring to Damascus, cf. v. 10), but in reality the enemy was the sin nature of the covenant people (all people).
This reminds me of the prayer in Ps. 19:12-13.

▣ "Though I fall I will rise" The VERB (BDB 877, KB 1086) is a Qal PERFECT. This
could refer to individual restoration or the corporate restoration (i.e. Ezekiel 37) from the Exile (possibly purposeful ambiguity, cf. Micah 4:13).

▣ "Though I dwell in darkness" The VERB (BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERFECT)
means "to sit" or "to dwell." It is imagery for the current difficult situation.

Darkness is used often in the OT as the opposite of "light." This term can refer to an eschatological
situation (e.g. Isa. 9:1; 29:18). The author feels cut off from YHWH because of the corporate sin and the resulting judgment (cf. Isa. 6:5).
The worst aspect of judgment is the absence of YHWH's personal presence!

Special Topic: Darkness, I.

▣ "the Lord is a light for me" This is striking biblical imagery for

- truth versus falsehood

- healing and health versus rottenness and corruption

- moral goodness versus evil

- joy versus gloom

Notice this verse personifies this Light as God (cf. Ps. 27:1; Isa. 60:20; 1 Tim. 6:16; 1 John 1:5). Knowing Him,
obeying Him, serving Him forms believers' personal relationship with God (i.e. same personification is found in John 14:6).

In Isa. 9:2 people will see a great light and a light will shine on them (also note Ps. 139:11-12). This Messianic light is Jesus
(cf. John 8:12; 12:35-36,46). Verse 8 highlights YHWH's presence with the faithful in times of distress, while Micah 7:9 promises
a future day of personal physical encounter.

7:9 "Because I have sinned against Him" Micah (like Moses, Isaiah, and Daniel) acts as a representative
of the people. Notice all sin is against God! Personal disaster, as well as corporate disaster, is directly related to our individual and corporate
rebellion against YHWH (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-28)! Many godly Judeans will suffer because of their rebellious society.

Again there is the fluidity between "I" (NASB) and "we" (TEV). This prophet is acknowledging the
sin of his society (cf. Isa. 6:5). Sin is the problem, exile the result, but restoration is the sure hope and promise of the covenant God!

▣ "Until He pleads my case" This legal imagery is also seen in Micah 6:1-5. In different passages YHWH acts as

- a prosecuting attorney (e.g. Micah 6:2)

- a defense attorney (Micah 7:9)

- as well as judge

This is similar to the heavenly advocate in Job 5:1; 9:33;16:19; 33:27. This heavenly defense advocate is the
counterpoint to the heavenly adversary in Job 1-2. In Job the revelation of a future Davidic king is not yet revealed, but this is
exactly what Jesus did (i.e. John 10; 1 John 3:8)

▣ "He will bring me out to the light" This is a play on YHWH as light in Micah 7:8 line 3. God is light and
He brings truth to light (cf. Ps. 37:6).

character as Merciful Father is also seen in His forgiveness and restoration (i.e. forensic justification by grace through
faith, i.e. Eph. 2:8-9). He will make good His promises to the faithful remnant and to all humanity (i.e. Gen. 3:15)! This is similar to Job's
statement in Job 19:25-27 (see my exegetical, verse-by-verse commentary free online).

7:10 "Then my enemy will see" The VERB (BDB 906, KB 1157) is JUSSIVE in form, but
IMPERFECT in meaning. True revelation will be revealed to all at the time of YHWH's victorious coming.

Special Topic: The Second Coming

▣ "Where is the Lord your God" All ancient wars involved the national gods. The
Jews were confused in their theology concerning YHWH's help on behalf of "the nations" who judged His people (cf. Habakkuk).
YHWH used godless nations to bring His rebellious people back to Himself. Yet, He will also judge those nations (i.e. Assyria,
Babylon) which He used.

At first the Jews would have thought that the gods of these pagan nations were stronger than YHWH,
but the reality was that it was their sin (cf. Micah 7:9), not YHWH's impotence, that caused their demise. YHWH will vindicate
His name (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36) by also judging the invading nations (cf. Micah 7:13).

▣ "she will be trampled down,

Like mire of the streets" The CONSTRUCT "mud of the streets"
(BDB 376 and 299) is often used as imagery of defeat (e.g. 2 Sam. 22:43; Ps. 18:42; Zech. 10:5), as is the phrase "lick the
dust" in Micah 7:17 (cf. Isa. 49:23).

7:11 This verse seems to refer to the city of Jerusalem, however, the phrase for "building your walls"
(BDB 124 and 154 CONSTRUCT) is not usually used for city walls (cf. Amos 9:11), but for boundary
markers (e.g. Isa. 54:11). So, the capital may be imagery for all the people of God.

The "walls of the city" was an idiom referring to its security. YHWH will restore His people's land
and confidence in Himself.

7:12 "they will come to you" There have been three major theories as to how to interpret this verse:

- the Jews returning home from the Exile

- all the nations coming with tribute to the restored people of God

- Israel's ideal boundaries (v. 12d)

7:17 "They will lick the dust like a serpent,

Like reptiles of the earth" There are two basic possibilities:

- kissing the victor's feet (cf. Ps. 72:9; Isa. 49:23, this was a Hebrew idiom of military defeat). Foreign nations
characterized as snakes (cf. Jer. 8:17).

- symbol of elvil being defeated (cf. Gen. 3:14)

- unclean animals (cf. Lev. 11)

The question is whether this verse

- simply records the fear of the nations in light of YHWH's power and love for Israel

- describes the conversion of the nations

In context option #1 fits best, but in light of the NT option #2 fits best.

Special Topic: Monotheism

▣ "who pardons" This common Hebrew VERB (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal
PARTICIPLE) has the connotations of

- to lift up (e.g. Micah 4:1)

- to carry (e.g. Micah 6:16; 7:9)

- to take away (e.g. Micah 2:2)

- to pardon (e.g. Hosea 1:6; 14:2)

There is a series of phrases in Micah 7:18 which describe YHWH's graciousness and forgiveness
(cf. Ps. 103:12; Isa. 1:18; 38:17; 43:25; 44:22; Micah 7:19). When God forgives, He forgets!

The parallel VERB "passes over" (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal PARTICIPLE)
means "to pass over," "to pass through" (e.g. Micah 2:13; Amos 5:17) in the sense of "to overlook" (i.e. out of sight,
out of mind, cf. Micah 7:19). This same VERB is used in Amos 7:8 and 8:2 in a judgment sense. Only here
and in Prov. 19:22 does it have the sense of forgiveness.

Special Topic: Forgiveness in the OT

▣ The UBS Translator's Handbook on the Books of Obadiah and Micah points out that several
Hebrew words for sin are used in Micah 7:18-19:

- iniquity (BDB 730, i.e. to twist)

- transgression (BDB 833, i.e. to rebel)

- sins (BDB 308, i.e. to miss the mark)

The point being that all of the covenant people's covenant violations are forgiven (p. 191).

▣ "the remnant" this is a recurrent theme (cf. Micah 2:12; 4:7; 5:7,8).

PERFECT) means "to take hold of so as to retain" (cf. Exod. 9:2). This is an anthropomorphic phrase
which describes YHWH as a parent who punishes His children, but does not reject them and longs to restore
fellowship (cf. Ps. 103:8; Heb. 12:5-13).

7:20 "truth. . .unchanging love" The two characteristics of YHWH are to be reproduced in His people.

- "Truth" (BDB 54) in the OT implies trustworthiness or faithfulness (see
Special Topic: Believe, Trust, Faith and Faithfulness in the OT).

- "Hesed" (BDB 338 I) or covenant faithfulness (cf. Micah 6:8; see Special Topic: Lovingkindness).

God will produce a people of righteousness (i.e. not by performance, cf. Jer. 31:31-34, as in the OT,
but by His mercy and grace, cf. Ezek. 36:22-38, as in the NT, i.e. Eph. 2:8-9).

▣ "Jacob. . .Abraham. . .our forefathers" There was a relationship between God and His people that
was unique in its promises and in its obligations. There are two modern liturgical uses of this context in the synagogue.

- Verses 18-20, along with the book of Jonah, were read on the Day of Atonement in the Synagogue.

- On the afternoon of New Years day Orthodox Jews go to a place of running water and empty their
pockets while reciting Micah 7:18-20. This is called Tashlich or "thou will cast." It emphasizes not
only the covenant responsibility (i.e. removal of all sin), but also the mercy of God!

The theological issue in this context is not only God's gracious character, but the shocking addition
of a new covenant in Christ (cf. John 14:6). Is Israel saved by covenant obedience or by restoration to Canaan? The real
issue is the validity of the radical new message of Jesus (cf. John 14:6; Rom. 2:28-29; 9-11; Gal. 3; 6:16).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Is this chapter written for an individual or for a member of the corporate community?

- Define the Hebrew word hesed.

- Explain the contrast between Micah 7:7 and 8 and Micah 7:1-6.

- Why is the question of Micah 7:10 so important in light of the condition of the people of God?

- List the gracious characteristics of God in Micah 7:18 and 19.
